prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

More than a hundred dollars of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass things to stuff them in. Now a white and purple cloud is breathing in each corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table— each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I watch children shuffle strictly in line, cradle candles that dribbled hot white on their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad? Didn't I use to go mucking through streambeds with the skunk cabbage raising bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies and smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights have to be not switched on. And in close darkness the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does. I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring and one tall room and the tremble of my phone. I'm not the only one that love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being ripped to prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun I feel I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: More, Now, Didn

outputs.L1:
More than a hundred dollars’ worth of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass vessels to hold them. Now a white-and-purple cloud breathes in every corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills across my dining table—each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush.

Didn’t I watch children shuffle solemnly in line, cradling candles that dribbled hot white wax onto their fingers, chanting in Latin—just to fashion Sevilla’s Easter? Wasn’t I sad? Didn’t I once go mucking through streambeds as the skunk cabbage raised its bursting violet spears?

Look: the afternoon dies as night begins in the hearts of the lilies, then smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights must remain off. In the close darkness, the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does.

I know I’m not the only one whose life is a conditional clause, hanging from something to do with spring, one tall room, and the tremble of my phone. I’m not the only one whom love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being torn into prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun, I feel as though I have been falling headfirst for decades.

God, I am so transparent. So light.
outputs.L2:
They cost me over a hundred dollars. Utter foolishness. Then I had to hunt for more glass containers to hold them. In every corner of my beloved room, a cloud of white and violet now seems to breathe. Flowers cascade across the dining table, every bright, open face pressing tender leaves into the crowded arrangement.

Hadn’t I seen children move in rigid single file, carrying candles whose hot white wax ran over their fingers, reciting Latin to help create Easter in Sevilla? Hadn’t sorrow filled me? And didn’t I once wade through muddy creek beds while skunk cabbage thrust up purple spears ready to burst?

See how afternoon gives way to evening inside the lilies, how darkness rises like smoke through their trumpet-shaped throats until it floods the room, leaving no need to turn on the lights. In that intimate dimness, the fragrance becomes so intensely sweet that it seems capable of cutting me apart. And it does.

Surely I am not alone in feeling that my life is an unfinished condition, suspended from some connection among spring, a single high-ceilinged room, and the quiver of my phone. Surely I am not the only person whom love turns into twelve sheets snapping in the air, torn by the wind into flags of devotion. Standing in direct sunlight, I feel as though I have spent decades plunging downward, skull first. God, I am nearly see-through—almost weightless.
outputs.L3:
On impulse, the speaker spends more than a hundred dollars on flowers, bringing home enough blossoms to fill the entire room. Their abundance transforms the space and awakens vivid memories: the solemn Easter rituals of Sevilla, with their flowers and religious intensity, and childhood excursions through patches of blooming skunk cabbage. The flowers thus connect distant places and different stages of the speaker’s life.

As evening settles in, the room darkens and the lilies release an almost overpowering fragrance. Surrounded by their scent, the speaker feels emotionally exposed, as though the flowers have stripped away every defense. Spring, the intimacy of a beloved room, and the tense expectation of a phone call all become bound together in a moment of suspended uncertainty. Waiting seems to place life itself on hold.

Within this atmosphere, love is experienced not as comfort or stability but as a force that makes the speaker profoundly vulnerable. It leaves them fragile, weightless, and transparent—without anything solid to hold on to. The speaker feels caught in an endless fall, suspended between hope and fear, unable to know where or how they will land.
outputs.L4:
I filled the room with lilies because I did not know what else to do with my longing. Their white blossoms crowded the tables and windowsills, leaned from glass vases, and opened above the mantel like extravagant declarations. Gold pollen dusted their throats. Their green stems bent under the weight of so much beauty, and the petals—cool, waxen, almost luminous—seemed too lavish for an ordinary room. Yet sadness remained among them, quiet and persistent, inhabiting the spaces between each bloom.

The lilies carried spring indoors. Their fragrance summoned damp earth, rain-dark paths, and gardens stirring after winter. It recalled ceremonies in which flowers stood beside candles and polished vessels, offering purity, grief, and hope without distinguishing among them. I remembered hands arranging blossoms for altars and graves, for celebrations and promises. The same flowers seemed able to bless every threshold: birth, devotion, mourning, love.

All afternoon I moved among them, straightening a stem here, lifting a fallen petal there, as if order might protect me from what I felt. I imagined you entering the room and stopping at the sight of them. Perhaps you would understand that their abundance was not confidence but vulnerability made visible. Each flower said what I could not: that I had waited, that I was afraid, that hope had become almost indistinguishable from pain.

When evening came, the room changed. The lilies faded into pale shapes while their perfume deepened, freed from the distraction of color. Darkness made their presence more powerful. The air grew dense and sweet, and every breath seemed to draw them further into me. I could no longer tell whether the fragrance comforted or overwhelmed me. It filled my chest until I felt split open, exposed to every memory and every possible future.

Yet in that surrender, something unexpected happened. The heaviness began to lift. My body seemed to lose its boundaries, becoming transparent as glass and nearly weightless. Longing no longer felt like a burden I carried alone; it became the atmosphere around me, shared by the lilies, the darkened room, and the imagined nearness of you.

I still did not know whether you would come, or what love would ask of us if you did. But certainty no longer seemed necessary. Surrounded by flowers whose beauty was inseparable from their fragility, I understood that love does not always resolve doubt. Sometimes it transforms doubt into openness. Sometimes it asks only that we stop resisting—that we breathe in the darkness, allow ourselves to be changed, and yield to what we cannot yet name.
outputs.L5:
**More, Now, Didn’t**

She always wanted **more**—more time, more courage, more reasons to begin. But **now**, standing at the edge of everything familiar, she understood that waiting had been her only real mistake. She **didn’t** know what would happen next, but for the first time, uncertainty felt like freedom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about impulsively spending over a hundred dollars on flowers, filling a beloved room with them, and being overwhelmed by their beauty and fragrance as evening falls.
counterfactuals.output:
I spent one hundred and thirty-seven dollars on flowers as if money were only another kind of weather, passing briefly through my hands. I bought peonies tight as secrets, roses the color of dusk, lilies with their pale, extravagant throats, and armfuls of freesia, sweet peas, tulips leaning every way at once. I carried them home in rustling paper and filled the beloved room—every vase, every jar, the blue pitcher with the chipped lip, even the drinking glass beside the window.

By evening, the room had become a garden dreaming indoors. Blossoms crowded the table and mantelshelf, bent over books, brushed the curtains with their soft heads. The last light entered gold and left violet. Fragrance gathered in the corners, thickened above the floorboards, moved through me like a beautiful ache.

I sat among them, astonished by what I had done, poorer and somehow lavishly alive. Everywhere I looked, beauty was opening past reason. The flowers gave themselves away without caution. Their perfume rose as the shadows rose, until I could scarcely breathe for loving the room, the hour, the brief impossible abundance of it all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem in a breathless, confessional voice that connects lilies, springtime, Holy Week in Seville, childhood memories, romantic anticipation, and the feeling of waiting for a phone call.
counterfactuals.output:
I bought lilies because the room was too quiet  
and now their white mouths keep opening  
as if they know something about resurrection  
I don’t—  

outside, spring is spending itself recklessly,  
orange blossom in the gutters, light  
climbing every balcony in Seville,  
and Holy Week drifts through the streets  
on shoulders and brass,  
candles sweating, drums entering the body  
where the body has tried not to remember.  

When I was eight I thought the Virgin  
was really crying, that wax could feel,  
that every hooded figure carried  
a private thunder under the cloth.  
My mother held my hand so tightly  
I mistook fear for love,  
or love for the fear of losing someone  
in a crowd.  

Now I keep setting my phone faceup  
beside the lilies.  
Now every small vibration is Easter.  
Now your name not appearing  
becomes its own procession—  
slow, elaborate, unbearable—  
and I confess I have imagined  
what I’ll say when you call,  
how casual I’ll sound,  
as if I haven’t been pacing  
from window to window,  
as if spring has not entered me  
with all its knives and incense,  
as if I am not still that child  
watching sorrow lifted high above the street,  
believing if we wait long enough  
the dead will speak,  
the flowers will forgive us,  
the bell will ring,  
the screen will bloom,  
and your voice—your voice—  
will finally carry me home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lush, surreal prose poem about someone arranging white and purple flowers around their home. Use rhetorical questions, vivid botanical imagery, long flowing sentences, and end with a sensation of transparency and weightlessness.
counterfactuals.output:
Who taught the hands to make a garden of a house, to carry moon-white peonies from room to room and settle them in blue bowls, while purple irises opened their ink-dark throats as though each vase concealed a small, astonished night?

Along the windowsill, they arranged lilacs in trembling constellations, lavender spilling its cool breath over the glass, white roses leaning toward their own reflections with the grave curiosity of swans; and in the kitchen, among the cups and silver spoons, they placed violets so dark they seemed gathered from beneath sleep, beside starry sprays of jasmine whose perfume loosened the walls from their foundations.

Was the hallway always this long, this green with imagined rain? Had the staircase always curled upward like the stem of some impossible flower? They tucked pale anemones into banisters, wound wisteria around lamps, crowned the quiet bed with foxglove and phlox, until every room began to bloom beyond its borders, until doors became petals and shadows filled with bees made of violet smoke.

Still they moved gently, carrying armful after armful—the white flowers luminous as unwritten letters, the purple ones bruised with dusk—asking no one: What grief requires such beauty? What absence drinks from so many vessels? What beloved ghost might return if the air were made sweet enough?

By evening, the house had vanished beneath blossoms, and they stood at its fragrant center as pollen drifted like golden snow; their fingers shone through the stems, their breath mingled with the breath of orchids, and slowly their body grew clear as rain in a glass, lighter than perfume, lighter than light, transparent and weightless.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally intense first-person piece in which an extravagant flower purchase prompts memories of candlelit religious processions and skunk cabbage growing in streambeds, while unrequited love makes the speaker feel suspended in uncertainty.
counterfactuals.output:
I spent half my rent on flowers.

Not roses—those would have confessed too much—but armfuls of peonies, ranunculus, foxglove, and white lilies with throats like small, astonished mouths. I carried them home in buckets, extravagant as a bride, though no one was waiting for me. Pollen dusted my coat. Petals brushed my face with the tenderness I had been refusing to name.

All evening, I arranged and rearranged them. The apartment filled with their wet, green breath until it felt less like a room than a chapel.

I remembered the candlelit processions of my childhood: bodies moving slowly through the dark, each flame trembling inside its paper shield. I remembered wax cooling over my knuckles and the hymns rising around me, hundreds of voices pleading with a silence they called holy. We walked as if our longing had a destination. We believed the road itself might answer us.

But what I remember most is leaving the procession afterward, wandering beyond the churchyard to where the stream worried its way through the woods. There, in the black mud, skunk cabbage thrust up its strange maroon hoods, rank and miraculous. It made its own heat. It bloomed while frost still held the ground. I loved it for that—for being ugly, alive, and early; for announcing itself when the world was not ready.

I wish I had its courage.

Instead, I wait for you in every silence. I read mercy into your smallest kindnesses. A message becomes a candle. A glance becomes a procession. I follow each flicker until it gutters, and then I stand in the dark pretending darkness is only another kind of promise.

You do not love me. Or you do not love me enough. Or you might, someday, under some weather neither of us can name.

That “might” is where I live now: suspended between frost and thaw, between prayer and reply, between the hand reaching out and the hand withdrawn. Below me, the stream keeps moving. Above me, every candle shakes.

Around me, the flowers open with unbearable certainty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poetic monologue about spring, flowers, darkness, scent, and longing. Include lilies spilling over a dining table, a trembling phone, and a metaphor comparing love to bedsheets torn into prayer flags by the wind.
counterfactuals.output:
Spring comes softly, but never without ruin.

It enters through the open window carrying wet earth, crushed violets, and the dark green scent of things returning. On the dining table, lilies spill from a porcelain vase—white throats open, pollen burning gold against the cloth—as if the garden has leaned too far into the house and cannot pull itself back.

Outside, evening gathers beneath the trees. Darkness does not fall; it flowers. It unfolds petal by petal, filling the rooms with shadows and the faint perfume of rain.

Beside my hand, the phone trembles.

For one breath, I believe it is you.

That is how longing lives: not as an absence, but as a small bright animal startled awake by every sound. I have tried to quiet it. I have closed the windows, thrown out the dead stems, washed your scent from my clothes. Still, love returns—love like bedsheets torn into prayer flags by the wind, each white scrap snapping above the empty streets, asking the sky for what it cannot give back.

And spring, cruel with blossoms, keeps answering in flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
